event_overview.title: About US-Canada Trade Relations
event_overview.subject: US-Canada Trade Relations
event_overview.summary: U.S.-Canada trade relations are a long-running, highly integrated economic relationship governed principally by the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), known in Canada as CUSMA. The relationship combines broad duty-free trade and cross-border supply chains with recurring disputes over tariffs, market access, and sector-specific rules, including steel, aluminum, autos, agriculture, and regulatory measures.

facts.label: Governing agreement
facts.value: The United States and Canada, together with Mexico, are parties to the USMCA/CUSMA, which replaced NAFTA and entered into force on July 1, 2020.

facts.label: Participants and format
facts.value: USMCA/CUSMA is a trilateral trade agreement among the United States, Canada, and Mexico; it establishes rules for goods, services, customs procedures, rules of origin, labor, environment, digital trade, and dispute settlement.

facts.label: Economic context
facts.value: Canada is one of the United States' largest trading partners, with especially integrated automotive, energy, textile, and agricultural supply chains.

facts.label: Review mechanism
facts.value: The agreement provides for a joint review every six years; the first CUSMA joint review was scheduled for July 1, 2026.

facts.label: Areas of friction
facts.value: Despite the agreement, the two governments may impose or challenge trade measures outside ordinary preferential tariff treatment; recent official materials identify disputes and countermeasures involving steel, aluminum, automobiles, dairy access, and other non-tariff barriers.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows a narrow set of reported 2026 negotiation and tariff-escalation developments; it does not attempt to cover the full history of U.S.-Canada commerce, all USMCA/CUSMA disputes, or every bilateral policy issue.
